Md. Arshad Ali

full_judgment:
15. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, however, next contends that he is not arguing for a remand of the appeal to the appellate Court below for a rehearing without taking into consideration Exts C, D and G. He submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed a fundamental error of law apparent on the face of the record by completely shifting the onus of proof on the plaintiff, whereas it is for the defendants to prove that the power of attorney was false, forged and fabricated. He submits that on the back of the first page of the registered Deed of Exchange Ext. 2 the Sub-Registrar has clearly made an endorsement that a general power of attorney executed by Jagadish Chandra Gope and others dated 15.1.63 and attested by Attache, Pakistan Deputy High Commissioner Calcutta bearing Power No. 202/63 dated 16.1.63 was produced before him on 28.3.63. Mr. Shafique Ahmed submits that the plaintiff has discharged his initial onus of proving that his predecessor's title deed Ext. 2 was executed and registered by virtue of a power of attorney dated 15.1.63 executed by Jagadish Chandra Gope and 4 others. He submits that it has been held in the case of Rai Bahadur Chottey Lal Vs. The Collector of Moradabad A.I.R. 1922 (P.C.) 279 that the fad that the presentation is accepted by the Sub-Registrar as in proper form is prima facie evidence that the conditions have been satisfied ; and after such acceptance, the burden of proving any alleged informality rests on the person who challenges the registration. Mr. Shafique Ahmed also relied upon the case of Mohammad Chiragh Vs. Fatta and others. A.I.R. 1934 Lah 452, where it has been held that there is a presumption in law that all official acts regularly performed and when a document is accepted by the Sub-Registrar as duly presented, there is an initial presumption that the document was duly presented and that the person presenting it was duly authorised to do so. 

 16. In this particular case, Mr. Shafique Ahmed submits, the power of attorney executed by Jagadish and 4 others dated 15.1.63 was presented before the Sub-Registrar on 28.3.63 for the purpose of registering the Deed of Exchange Ext.2. There will be a presumption, he submits, that the persons presenting it were duly authorised to do. Thereafter it is for the defendants to prove that the plaintiff was not so authorised. Mr. Shafique Ahmed submits that the defendants have adduced no evidence to that effect, except the additional evidence in Ext. D which is not admissible. Mr. Shafique Ahmed further submits that the loss of the original power of attorney is totally irrelevant. Once the plaintiff submits the endorsement on the back of the first page of Ext. 2 the burden of proof shifted to the defendants. They have to prove that the power of attorney was forged. 

 17. In reply Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that reading sections 32-35 of the Registration Act together, there is no doubt that some presumption will arise when a power of attorney is presented before a Sub-Registrar. But he maintains that the presumption is only this much that the power of attorney was executed before the Sub-Registrar and authenticated by the person or Court before whom it was executed and authenticated. There is no presumption that The persons whose names occur was executors of the power of attorney and executed the same. Mr. Mahmudul Islam reinforces his argument by referring to section 85 of the Evidence Act and submitting that in this section also the presumption attached to a power of attorney does not extend beyond the fact that it was executed before and authenticated by the person or Court concerned. Making a reference to Section 90 of the Evidence Act Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that in this section the legislature desired that private documents would carry presumptions of a bigger dimension. It has used appropriate language to that effect. Section 90 of the Evidence Act provides that in the case of document, at belt a private document of thirty years old, the presumption is that the signature and hand-writing purporting to be that of a particular person is in that person's handwriting and signature. The presumption even extends to the fact that it was duly executed and attested by the person by whom it purports to be executed and attested. Mr. Islam submits that if a private document like a power of attorney is to be given a presumption as wide as claimed by the plaintiff petitioner, then the legislature would have conferred wider presumptions in Sections 32-35 of the Registration Act and in Section 85 of the Evidence Act. Mr. Islam submits that in the Privy Council decision referred to by Mr. Shafique Ahmed the presumption extends only upto the fact that the power of attorney was in the proper form. In the case cited from the Lahore High Court the presumption was carried to the extent not supported by the decision of the Privy Council. Mr. Mahmudul Islam further submits that if the presumption is carried so far as to presume that the person who presented the power of attorney was authorised to do so, then the burden of proof will fall upon those who will challenge the power of attorney including unwary owners of land who never executed any power of attorney and it will be well-nigh impossible on the part of the affected persons to discharge that onus where the power of attorney is executed and registered in foreign countries and also when the power of attorney is withheld from evidence. 

 "So far as the scope of this section 85 of the Evidence Act is concerned, it is plain that the law ask the court to presume due execution and authentication of a power of attorney, Wit is so done, amongst others, by a Pakistan Consul or Vice-Consul. In the particular case it was clone by the Deputy High Commissioner of Pakistan in Calcutta. It is also to be observed that the execution does include not merely bare signature of the donor, but a signature indicating the due completion of the transaction. Authentication under the section is not mere attestation. It comprehends that the person authenticating it has assured himself of the identity of the donor who has signed the instrument, as well as the fact of execution. It is for this reason that the presumption under the section, unless rebutted, stands, and the document can be admitted in evidence as a document executed by the person alleged to have executed it, without any further proof. A reading of the section gives two result. A power of attorney fulfilling the conditions of the section raises a presumption of due execution and authentication without further proof and secondly, the onus of rebuttal, as a necessary corollary, lies on the person who challenges it (vide Wali Mohammad. Chaudhari Vs. Jamaluddin Chaudhari A.I.R. 1930 Allahabad 524 and Jagraj Singh Vs. Jaswant Singh 1971 (1) S.C.A. 136 A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 76)".
